title: fetch_user retries transient network errors
tldr: `fetch_user` now tries up to three times when the network times out or drops, waiting a little longer each time. The config change doubles the learning-rate warmup.

intents.text: Retry `fetch_user` when CI hits a network timeout
intents.quote: fetchUser fails randomly in CI. Add a retry.

intents.text: Do not retry when the user does not exist
intents.evidence: Only `TimeoutError` and `ConnectionError` retry, so an HTTP 404 is never caught here. Whether the client raises on 404 at all is not visible in this diff.

unasked.text: The learning-rate warmup doubles from 500 to 1000 steps. No request in the session mentions it.

diagrams.caption: A failed call loops back until the attempts run out; only the last failure reaches the caller.

frames.caption: After: the call sits inside a loop of up to three attempts.
The third failure is re-raised, so the caller still sees the error.

background.deep: A **transient** error is one that may succeed if you simply try again, such as a timeout. A **permanent** error, such as asking for a user that does not exist, fails the same way every time. Retrying a permanent error only wastes time.
background.narrow: `fetch_user` in [[src/fetch.py:6-14]] wraps one HTTP GET through a `client` object. Before this change it made exactly one call and let any exception escape.

intuition: Picture CI calling `fetch_user(client, 42)` while the network blips. Attempt 1 times out, the code sleeps 0.1 s; attempt 2 times out, it sleeps 0.2 s; attempt 3 succeeds and returns the JSON. If attempt 3 had also failed, the error would reach the caller exactly as before, just 0.3 s later.

steps.title: Name the errors worth retrying
steps.body: A module-level tuple lists the two exception types that count as transient. Everything else, including whatever the client raises for a missing user, escapes on the first attempt.

steps.title: Wrap the call in a bounded loop
steps.body: The new `attempts=3` parameter bounds the loop. `range(1, attempts + 1)` counts attempts from 1, which makes the last-attempt check read naturally: `attempt == attempts` re-raises instead of sleeping.

steps.title: Wait a little longer each time
steps.body: The sleep grows linearly: 0.1 s after the first failure, 0.2 s after the second. With three attempts the worst case adds 0.3 s before the final error.

steps.title: Double the learning-rate warmup
steps.body: `optimizer.warmup_steps` goes from 500 to 1000. Nothing in `src/` reads it, so it does not interact with the retry change.

quiz.stem: The client raises `TimeoutError` on attempts 1 and 2, then returns normally. How long does `fetch_user` sleep in total?

options.feedback: That counts a sleep after the successful third attempt too. The `return` exits the loop before any sleep.
It sleeps 0.1 s after attempt 1 and 0.2 s after attempt 2. Attempt 3 returns, so there is no third sleep.
That is only the second sleep. The first failure also sleeps, for 0.1 s.

quiz.stem: Suppose the `if attempt == attempts: raise` lines were deleted. What happens when all three attempts time out?

options.feedback: `range(1, attempts + 1)` still ends after three iterations. The loop is bounded by the range, not by the raise.
The `except` clause catches it and then sleeps. Without the explicit `raise`, nothing re-raises it.
The loop finishes without a `return` or a `raise`, so Python returns `None`. The caller gets no error and no data.

quiz.stem: When would retrying every exception, not just the two in `RETRYABLE`, be the better choice?

options.feedback: If no error can be permanent, catching everything costs nothing. Here a missing user is permanent, so retrying it would only delay the same failure.

options.text: When the sleep is very short
options.feedback: A short sleep makes wasted retries cheaper, but they are still wasted for permanent errors. The type of error decides, not the delay.

options.text: When attempts is set to one
options.feedback: With one attempt nothing is retried at all, so the choice of exceptions no longer matters.

tryIt.title: Watch it survive two timeouts
tryIt.predict: A fake client fails twice with `TimeoutError`, then succeeds. Predict the printed result and the number of calls.
tryIt.lookFor: The dict and the call count on one line.
tryIt.expect: `{'id': 42} 3`: two failed calls, then the third returns.

unknowns: Whether the real client raises `TimeoutError` or wraps it in its own exception type. If it wraps it, nothing retries.
